lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you met community helpers. What do we call people who help without being paid? (Volunteers.) Today: charities and voluntary groups, what they do, and how you can help.

A charity is an organisation set up to help a good cause, not to make a profit for owners. Causes include health, children, animals, the environment, education, homelessness and help after disasters. England and Wales have over 170,000 registered charities.

Charities raise money from donations, fundraising events, charity shops, grants and gifts left in wills. In the UK, Gift Aid lets a charity claim back tax: for every 4 gold a taxpayer gives, it can claim 1 more. Many also rely on volunteers' time.

Charities in the past changed lives. In 1863 Henry Dunant helped start the Red Cross, after seeing wounded soldiers left without help. In 1870 Thomas Barnardo opened a home in London for children with nowhere to live.

Before giving, check: is it a registered charity? How much does it spend on its work, compared with fundraising and running costs? Can it show what it has achieved? Be careful of fake charity messages: grade 6's scam checks still apply.

There are many ways to help besides money: volunteering time, sharing a skill, giving things you no longer need, raising awareness, or helping a neighbour. Voluntary groups, such as sports clubs and faith groups, also do much for communities.

Choosing a cause is personal. Ask: what do I care about? Where can my help do most good: nearby or far away? Some people give to big causes; others help one local group. Either way, small gifts add up when many people give.
Try it in the world: set up a charity stall in your village. Choose a cause and make a sign saying what the gold will do. Keep an honest record of what you raise and spend. Next: media and bias.

exercises.hint: It is not run to make money for owners.
choices: an organisation helping a good cause
exercises.explain: An organisation set up to help a good cause, not to make a profit for owners.

exercises.prompt: Which is a way to help without giving money?
exercises.hint: What else can you give besides gold?
exercises.explain: Volunteering your time, or sharing a skill.

exercises.prompt: Charities are set up to make a profit for their owners.
exercises.hint: Where does a charity's money go?
exercises.explain: False: a charity's money goes to its cause.

exercises.prompt: Who helped start the Red Cross in 1863?
exercises.hint: He had seen wounded soldiers left without help.
exercises.explain: Henry Dunant helped start the Red Cross in 1863, after seeing wounded soldiers left without help.

exercises.hint: Where do its things come from?
choices: a shop selling given items to raise money
a shop where everything is free
exercises.explain: A shop that sells donated items and gives the money to its cause.

exercises.prompt: A charity raised 8,000 gold and spent 90% of it on its work. How much went to its work?
With Gift Aid, a charity gets 1 gold more for every 4 given. Zara gives 20 gold. How much does the charity get in all?
exercises.hint: Find a quarter of the gift, then add it on.

exercises.prompt: Before giving to a charity, what is wise to check?
exercises.hint: Think of scams, and of where the gold goes.
choices: that it is registered and what it spends
exercises.explain: Check that it is a registered charity and how much it spends on its work.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: a gift of money or things
exercises.hint: Two are gifts, one is a person, one is an event.
exercises.explain: Donation: a gift. Volunteer: gives time. Fundraiser: an event. Grant: money from another body.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: giving money, or giving time?
items: a gift left in a will
exercises.hint: Is gold handed over, or hours of help?
exercises.explain: Money: the donation, the sponsored walk, the will. Time: the food bank, reading, coaching.

exercises.prompt: Charity A spent 90% of 5,000 gold on its work; Charity B spent 60% of 7,000 gold. How much more did A spend on its work than B?
exercises.hint: Work out each charity's amount first.

exercises.prompt: Two charities raised the same amount. One spent 90% on its work, the other 60%. Which did more of its work?
exercises.hint: Compare the shares of the same amount.
exercises.explain: 90% of the same amount is more than 60%, so the first did more of its work.

exercises.prompt: A message asking you to send gold to a charity you have never heard of can always be trusted.
exercises.explain: False: check it is a registered charity, and tell a grown-up, before giving.

exercises.hint: What if a thousand people each give a little?
choices: they add up when many people give
exercises.explain: Small gifts from many people add up to a lot.

exercises.prompt: Tilly wants to help animals near her home. Which is the best choice?
choices: volunteer at a local animal rescue
send gold to a stranger online
buy a pet on a whim
exercises.explain: Volunteering at a local animal rescue helps the animals she cares about, near home.
